title: Emotion Coaching Parents
text:
John Gottman, Lynn Katz and Carole Hooven wanted to know how parents' attitudes toward emotions shape their children. They studied families with young children, interviewing each parent at length about their own feelings and how they responded to their children's sadness and anger. They called this a parent's meta-emotion philosophy: their feelings about feelings.

Some parents tended to dismiss children's negative emotions. They distracted the child, minimized the problem, or wanted the feeling to pass quickly. Others were critical, punishing the child for showing anger or sadness. A third group, which the researchers called emotion coaching parents, did something different. They noticed even mild emotions in their children, saw them as a chance for closeness and teaching, helped the child put a name to the feeling, listened with empathy, and set limits on behavior while helping the child solve the problem.

The researchers followed the children for several years. Children whose parents practiced emotion coaching were better at calming themselves when upset, as shown even in measures of their physiology. By around age eight they also did better in school, got along better with other children and had fewer behavior problems.

Gottman later popularized these findings in his book Raising an Emotionally Intelligent Child.
lesson: A child's anger or sadness is a chance to connect and teach, not a problem to shut down. Name the feeling, empathize, and then help solve the problem.
people: John Gottman, Lynn Katz, Carole Hooven
source: Gottman, J. M., Katz, L. F., and Hooven, C. (1996). Parental meta-emotion philosophy and the emotional life of families: Theoretical models and preliminary data. Journal of Family Psychology, 10(3), 243-268.
caveat: The original sample was small and the results correlational, though later intervention studies of emotion coaching have reported encouraging results.
